# Case study: slope × alignment {#sec-m3-declividade}

The question of this chapter is a design question:

> *Given two alignment alternatives between the Curitiba plateau and the coast, which of them
> faces the more favourable terrain? What length of each exceeds the admissible gradient,
> and where are those stretches?*

It is the classic combination of **raster** data (the digital elevation model) and
**vector** data (the alignments). It is the operation the course programme describes as "crossing
slope with proposed alignments".

```{r}
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

crs_trabalho <- 31982
```

## Step 1: The terrain

```{r}
if (!file.exists("dados/brutos/dem_serra.tif")) {
  area <- sf::st_bbox(c(xmin = -49.40, ymin = -25.75, xmax = -48.40, ymax = -25.15),
                  crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) |> sf::st_as_sfc() |> sf::st_as_sf()
  terra::writeRaster(
    terra::rast(elevatr::get_elev_raster(locations = area, z = 11, clip = "bbox")),
    "dados/brutos/dem_serra.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
}

dem <- terra::rast("dados/brutos/dem_serra.tif") |> terra::project("EPSG:31982")
names(dem) <- "altitude"

declividade <- tan(terra::terrain(dem, v = "slope", unit = "radians")) * 100
names(declividade) <- "declividade"

c(resolucao_m = round(terra::res(dem)[1], 1),
  alt_min = round(terra::global(dem, "min", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  alt_max = round(terra::global(dem, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]))
```

::: {.callout-note}
Slope as a **percentage** is the road engineering convention (a 6% grade
rises 6 m for every 100 m of horizontal distance). `terra` also computes it in degrees
(`unit = "degrees"`), used in geomorphology. Do not mix the two in the same document.
:::

## Step 2: The alignments

Alternative 1 is the existing alignment of the BR-116, taken from OpenStreetMap. Alternative 2 is a
hypothetical alignment: the line someone would draw linking the same end points through another valley.

```{r}
if (!file.exists("dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg")) {
  consulta <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-49.40, -25.75, -48.40, -25.15), timeout = 120) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "ref", value = "BR-116") |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()
  sf::st_write(consulta$osm_lines |>
             dplyr::select(dplyr::any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway"))) |>
             sf::st_transform(4674),
           "dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
}

br116 <- sf::st_read("dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

# Overpass returns the whole geometry of each way, not clipped by the query's
# bbox. Without this filter, the longest segment may come from far away from the Serra
area_recorte <- sf::st_bbox(c(xmin = -49.40, ymin = -25.75, xmax = -48.40, ymax = -25.15),
                        crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) |> sf::st_as_sfc() |> sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)
br116 <- br116[sf::st_intersects(br116, area_recorte, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]

# alternative 1: the longest continuous segment of the BR-116 in the area
alt1 <- br116 |>
  dplyr::mutate(comp = as.numeric(sf::st_length(geom))) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(comp, n = 1) |>
  sf::st_geometry()

# alternative 2: hypothetical alignment between the same end points, by another route
extremos <- sf::st_cast(alt1, "POINT")
p_ini <- extremos[1]
p_fim <- extremos[length(extremos)]

desvio <- sf::st_point(colMeans(rbind(sf::st_coordinates(p_ini), sf::st_coordinates(p_fim))) +
                     c(4000, -6000))

alt2 <- sf::st_sfc(
  sf::st_linestring(rbind(sf::st_coordinates(p_ini), sf::st_coordinates(desvio),
                      sf::st_coordinates(p_fim))),
  crs = crs_trabalho
)

tracados <- sf::st_sf(
  alternativa = c("Alt. 1: existing alignment", "Alt. 2: hypothetical alignment"),
  geometry = c(alt1, alt2)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(extensao_km = round(as.numeric(sf::st_length(geometry)) / 1000, 1))

sf::st_drop_geometry(tracados)
```

Before any calculation, the two alignments over the satellite image. Switch the basemap in the
selector in the top-left corner to see the relief and the forest of the Serra:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(tracados, zcol = "alternativa", lwd = 4,
                 map.types = c("Esri.WorldImagery", "OpenStreetMap"),
                 layer.name = "Alignment")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Alternative 2 is a line made up for the exercise, with three vertices. A real alignment
comes from the geometric design, respecting minimum curve radius, maximum grade and the traverse
surveyed in the field. It arrives here as a *shapefile*. The analysis procedure, however, is
exactly the same, and that is what the chapter demonstrates.
:::

## Step 3: Segmenting the alignment

Slope is not a property of the whole alignment: it varies from stretch to stretch. That is why the
first analytical step is to **break each alignment into segments** of fixed length.

```{r}
segmentar <- function(linha, passo_m = 200) {
  comp <- as.numeric(sf::st_length(linha))
  n <- max(2, floor(comp / passo_m))

  pontos <- sf::st_line_sample(linha, n = n) |> sf::st_cast("POINT")
  coords <- sf::st_coordinates(pontos)

  segs <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(coords) - 1), \(i) {
    sf::st_linestring(coords[i:(i + 1), ])
  }) |>
    sf::st_sfc(crs = sf::st_crs(linha))

  sf::st_sf(seg_id = seq_along(segs), geometry = segs) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      comp_m = as.numeric(sf::st_length(geometry)),
      dist_acum_km = cumsum(comp_m) / 1000
    )
}

segmentos <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  segmentar(alt1) |> dplyr::mutate(alternativa = tracados$alternativa[1]),
  segmentar(alt2) |> dplyr::mutate(alternativa = tracados$alternativa[2])
)

dplyr::count(sf::st_drop_geometry(segmentos), alternativa)
```

## Step 4: Combining with the terrain

Two slope measures, which are worth computing and comparing:

1. the **terrain slope** under the segment, extracted from the raster;
2. the **grade of the alignment**, computed as the elevation difference between the ends of the segment
   divided by its length. That is what really matters for the design.

```{r}
segmentos <- segmentos |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # 1. mean terrain slope under the segment
    decliv_terreno = terra::extract(declividade, terra::vect(segmentos),
                                    fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)[[1]],
    # 2. grade of the alignment itself
    alt_ini = terra::extract(dem, terra::vect(sf::st_line_sample(geometry, sample = 0) |>
                                         sf::st_cast("POINT")), ID = FALSE)[[1]],
    alt_fim = terra::extract(dem, terra::vect(sf::st_line_sample(geometry, sample = 1) |>
                                         sf::st_cast("POINT")), ID = FALSE)[[1]],
    rampa_pct = 100 * (alt_fim - alt_ini) / comp_m
  )

segmentos |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    segmentos = dplyr::n(),
    extensao_km = round(sum(comp_m) / 1000, 1),
    decliv_terreno_media = round(mean(decliv_terreno, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    rampa_media_abs = round(mean(abs(rampa_pct), na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    rampa_max_abs = round(max(abs(rampa_pct), na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .by = alternativa
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Step 5: Classifying by design criterion

The maximum admissible grade depends on the highway class and on the terrain. Geometric design
manuals work with bands; we will use three simple, explicit classes:

```{r}
limite_desejavel <- 4    # %
limite_maximo    <- 6    # %

segmentos <- segmentos |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    classe = dplyr::case_when(
      abs(rampa_pct) <= limite_desejavel ~ "up to 4% (desirable)",
      abs(rampa_pct) <= limite_maximo    ~ "4% to 6% (admissible)",
      TRUE                               ~ "above 6% (critical)"
    ),
    classe = factor(classe, levels = c("up to 4% (desirable)", "4% to 6% (admissible)",
                                       "above 6% (critical)"))
  )

resumo <- segmentos |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(km = sum(comp_m) / 1000, .by = c(alternativa, classe)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = km / sum(km), .by = alternativa)

resumo |>
  dplyr::mutate(km = round(km, 1), part = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(alternativa, classe) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrr")
```

This is the table that answers the chapter's question. It is the format in which a result like this
goes into a technical note: length and share by grade band, for each alternative.

Where are the critical segments? Click on a segment to see the grade and the terrain
slope:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(segmentos, zcol = "classe", lwd = 5,
                 col.regions = c("#1a9850", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
                 color = c("#1a9850", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
                 map.types = c("Esri.WorldImagery", "OpenStreetMap"),
                 layer.name = "Alignment grade")
```

## Step 6: The profile and the map

```{r}
#| label: fig-perfil
#| fig-cap: "Elevation profile and grade per segment, for the two alternatives"
#| fig-height: 5.2
perfil <- segmentos |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::mutate(dist_km = dist_acum_km)

g1 <- ggplot(perfil, aes(dist_km, alt_ini, colour = alternativa)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1a5b8a", "#b3402a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Elevation (m)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

g2 <- ggplot(perfil, aes(dist_km, rampa_pct, colour = alternativa)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-6, -4, 4, 6), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1a5b8a", "#b3402a"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Distance along the alignment (km)", y = "Grade (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2, ncol = 1, heights = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mapa-declividade
#| fig-cap: "Alignments over the terrain slope; the critical segments highlighted"
#| fig-height: 5.4
recorte <- sf::st_bbox(sf::st_buffer(sf::st_union(tracados), 4000))

decliv_recorte <- terra::crop(declividade, terra::ext(recorte[c("xmin", "xmax", "ymin", "ymax")]))

ggplot() +
  tidyterra::geom_spatraster(data = decliv_recorte) +
  geom_sf(data = segmentos, aes(colour = classe), linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#f7f7f7", "#cfd8dc", "#8fa3ad", "#4d5c63"),
                       na.value = NA, name = "Terrain\nslope (%)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("up to 4% (desirable)" = "#1a9850",
                                 "4% to 6% (admissible)" = "#e0a03f",
                                 "above 6% (critical)" = "#b3402a"),
                      name = "Alignment grade") +
  coord_sf(xlim = recorte[c("xmin", "xmax")], ylim = recorte[c("ymin", "ymax")],
           expand = FALSE) +
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.25) +
  labs(caption = paste("Sources: elevation AWS Terrain Tiles (via elevatr);",
                       "road axis OpenStreetMap. Own elaboration.")) +
  theme_void(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## Step 7: Steep slopes along the mountain highways

The same slope raster answers another question, about operations rather than design:

> *Along the highways that already exist in the Serra, where does the road run next to steep
> slopes, which are the most prone to landslides?*

It is a concrete question in the Serra do Mar of Paraná: in November 2022, a slope
landslide on the BR-376, in Guaratuba, hit vehicles on the carriageway and closed the highway. We will do an **exploratory
analysis** of the two highways that descend the Serra in our area: the BR-277
(Curitiba–Paranaguá) and the PR-410, the Estrada da Graciosa.

::: {.callout-warning}
## This is not a susceptibility map

Landslide susceptibility depends on slope, but also on geology, soil,
vegetation cover, drainage, rainfall and cuttings made by the works themselves. Here we use **only
slope**, and from a DEM of about 70 m, which smooths the embankments by the road. The
result serves to point out stretches to look at first, not to classify risk. The official sources
are the **susceptibility maps for gravitational mass movements** by the Geological
Survey of Brazil (SGB/CPRM), Cemaden's alerts and the incident history of DNIT and the state
highway departments (DER).
:::

First, the highways. We download both from OpenStreetMap by the code in the `ref` field, as
we did with the BR-116. We crop the Serra zone and, since the BR-277 is a dual carriageway, we keep
one carriageway of each highway, so as not to count the length twice:

```{r}
if (!file.exists("dados/brutos/rodovias_serra_pr.gpkg")) {
  consulta <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-49.10, -25.62, -48.70, -25.30), timeout = 120) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "ref", value = c("BR-277", "PR-410")) |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()
  sf::st_write(consulta$osm_lines |>
             dplyr::select(dplyr::any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway"))) |>
             sf::st_transform(4674),
           "dados/brutos/rodovias_serra_pr.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
}

zona_serra <- sf::st_bbox(c(xmin = -49.10, ymin = -25.62, xmax = -48.70, ymax = -25.30),
                          crs = sf::st_crs(4326)) |>
  sf::st_as_sfc() |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

rodovias_serra <- sf::st_read("dados/brutos/rodovias_serra_pr.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::rename(geometry = geom) |>          # the GeoPackage calls the geometry "geom"
  dplyr::filter(ref %in% c("BR-277", "PR-410")) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho) |>
  sf::st_intersection(zona_serra) |>
  dplyr::group_by(ref) |>
  dplyr::summarise() |>                  # joins the segments of each highway
  sf::st_line_merge() |>
  sf::st_cast("LINESTRING")              # one line per carriageway

rodovias_serra |>
  dplyr::mutate(km = round(as.numeric(sf::st_length(geometry)) / 1000, 1)) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry()
```

```{r}
# the longest carriageway of each highway
rodovias_serra <- rodovias_serra |>
  dplyr::mutate(comp = as.numeric(sf::st_length(geometry))) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(comp, n = 1, by = ref)
```

Next, the criterion. Terrain slope is classified with two well-known thresholds:

| Slope | Reference |
|:--|:--|
| above 30% (≈ 17°) | threshold in Law 6,766/79 for urban land subdivision without specific requirements |
| above 47% (≈ 25°) | band in which susceptibility maps usually indicate high susceptibility |

```{r}
#| label: fig-encostas
#| fig-cap: "Terrain slope in the Serra zone, in three bands, and the highways analysed"
#| fig-height: 5
decliv_serra <- terra::crop(declividade, terra::vect(zona_serra))

faixas_decliv <- terra::classify(decliv_serra, rcl = matrix(c(
  -Inf, 30, 1,
    30, 47, 2,
    47, Inf, 3
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))

plot(faixas_decliv, type = "classes",
     levels = c("up to 30%", "30% to 47%", "above 47%"),
     col = c("#f0f0f0", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
     main = "Terrain slope in the Serra")
plot(terra::vect(rodovias_serra), add = TRUE, lwd = 2.5, col = "#1a5b8a")
```

Before measuring, it is worth checking on the interactive map that the crop is right: the Serra zone, the
slope bands (same colours as the figure above) and the two highways. Switch the basemap
to the satellite image and compare the slopes with the forest:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(zona_serra, alpha.regions = 0, color = "black", lwd = 2,
                 layer.name = "Serra zone", legend = FALSE) +
  mapview::mapview(faixas_decliv, col.regions = c("#f0f0f0", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
                   alpha.regions = 0.5, layer.name = "Slope (bands)", legend = FALSE) +
  mapview::mapview(rodovias_serra, zcol = "ref", lwd = 3,
                   color = c("#1a5b8a", "#7b3294"), layer.name = "Highways")
```

The measure for each stretch of highway: we split each carriageway into 200 m segments, with the same
`segmentar()` function from step 3, and look at a 150 m strip on each side. The question is **what
fraction of that strip has slopes above 30%**.

```{r}
segmentos_serra <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(rodovias_serra)), \(i) {
  segmentar(sf::st_geometry(rodovias_serra)[i], passo_m = 200) |>
    dplyr::mutate(ref = rodovias_serra$ref[i])
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()

# 150 m strip on each side of the segment, without rounded ends
faixa_150 <- sf::st_buffer(segmentos_serra, 150, endCapStyle = "FLAT")

# the mean of a 0/1 raster is the fraction of cells equal to 1
ingreme <- declividade > 30

segmentos_serra <- segmentos_serra |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    pct_ingreme  = 100 * terra::extract(ingreme, terra::vect(faixa_150),
                                        fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)[[1]],
    decliv_media = terra::extract(declividade, terra::vect(faixa_150),
                                  fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)[[1]],
    exposicao = cut(pct_ingreme, breaks = c(-Inf, 10, 50, Inf),
                    labels = c("low (< 10%)", "medium (10% to 50%)", "high (> 50%)"))
  )

segmentos_serra |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::select(ref, seg_id, dist_acum_km, pct_ingreme, decliv_media, exposicao) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(pct_ingreme, n = 6, with_ties = FALSE)
```

The segments at the top of the list are those in which most of the side strip is a steep
slope. The summary by highway:

```{r}
segmentos_serra |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(km = sum(comp_m) / 1000, .by = c(ref, exposicao)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = km / sum(km), .by = ref) |>
  dplyr::arrange(ref, exposicao) |>
  dplyr::mutate(km = round(km, 1), part = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Highway", "Exposure to steep slopes", "km", "Share"),
               align = "llrr")
```

Along each highway, the profile shows **where** these stretches are:

```{r}
#| label: fig-perfil-encostas
#| fig-cap: "Fraction of the side strip (150 m) with slope above 30%, along each highway"
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(sf::st_drop_geometry(segmentos_serra), aes(dist_acum_km, pct_ingreme)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = exposicao), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ref, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#cfd8dc", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Distance along the highway, in the Serra zone (km)",
       y = "% of the strip with slope > 30%") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

And on the map, over the satellite image, to check case by case. Turn on the slope layer
in the layer selector to see the slopes behind each stretch:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(faixas_decliv, col.regions = c("#f0f0f0", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
                 alpha.regions = 0.5, layer.name = "Slope band",
                 hide = TRUE, map.types = c("Esri.WorldImagery", "OpenStreetMap")) +
  mapview::mapview(segmentos_serra, zcol = "exposicao", lwd = 5,
                   color = c("#cfd8dc", "#e0a03f", "#b3402a"),
                   layer.name = "Exposure")
```

On the satellite image, the high-exposure stretches fall on the descent of the Serra, where the road
cuts across the forest-covered slope. That is where an inspection of embankments, drainage and retaining
structures would start. To become a study, this map would be combined with SGB's susceptibility map,
with accumulated rainfall and with the history of closures of each highway.

## What this case study showed

1. Combining raster × vector comes down to three functions: `terrain()` to derive the
   slope, `st_line_sample()` to segment, `extract()` to combine.
2. Distinguishing **terrain slope** from **alignment grade** changes the conclusion: an alignment
   can cross steep terrain with a gentle grade, which is what makes a good design.
3. The useful result is not the map: it is the table of length by grade band, which goes
   straight into the comparison of alternatives.
4. Every assumption (grade limit, slope bands) is written
   in a variable at the top of the block, not hidden in the middle of a calculation.
5. The same raster serves operations: segmenting an existing highway and measuring the slope beside
   each stretch points to where to look first. But an analysis with slope alone is
   exploratory; landslide risk is assessed with the official susceptibility maps.
